reading.title: Comparing historical labels
reading.text: In an architecture seminar, Lea compares historical labels rather than dates an unknown building by appearance alone. Greek and Roman traditions influenced later design. Byzantine, Romanesque and Gothic buildings developed distinct approaches, though buildings can combine features. Renaissance and Baroque are not interchangeable; Neoclassical refers to a later renewed use of classical forms. Beaux-Arts and Palladian describe other traditions of composition. Art Nouveau often uses flowing ornament, whereas Art Deco often uses stylized geometric decoration. The Bauhaus was a school founded in 1919; its influence extends beyond one building style. Modernist and Brutalist labels have different histories and emphases. Lea uses documented examples and asks which feature supports a comparison. One column, arch or concrete wall is insufficient to establish a complete historical classification.

reading.title: Separating styles from performance

High-Tech design emphasizes technological or structural expression; Minimalist design reduces elements. Sustainable design addresses wider environmental effects. Parametric design uses relationships between parameters, Organic design relates forms to context, and Biophilic design incorporates connections with nature. A smart building uses systems and controls. Adaptive reuse gives an existing building a new use. Net zero here concerns an annual energy balance under a specified definition; Passive House concerns a defined energy-performance approach. Modular construction uses separately made units. reading.title: Describing architectural elements
reading.text: Lea describes a building's parts before debating its style. A dome covers a space with a rounded form. An arch spans an opening, while a vault covers a longer space with an arched structure. A cantilever projects beyond its support. The facade is an exterior face of a building, not its complete plan. An atrium is a large interior space, often open through several levels, and a skylight admits light through the roof. A colonnade is a sequence of columns. A portico is a covered entrance or porch supported by columns. A minaret is a tower associated with a mosque. Lea compares these visible forms while respecting their context. The words describe elements and functions; they do not establish a building's age, location or certification.
